Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase its detection power while maintaining "false discovery rate" (FDR) within a predetermined threshold. Popular algorithms like the BH method struggle to control FDR, particularly when encountering positive dependence, which requires conservative estimations. In this paper, we propose new statistical approaches that can reliably and accurately calculate ATE, demonstrating their ability to effectively control FDR and boost detection power through both simulated and real-world experiments. Our methods are shown to work efficiently with robust and controlled FDR, while offering improved scalability. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis and comparison of our approach to other prominent FDR control methods like knockoff and the AdaPT procedure.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented.

The CDF II Collaboration has made a precise measurement of the W boson mass which, when compared to the Standard Model's predicted value, shows a significant discrepancy of approximately 7$\sigma$.  To determine the impact of the measured W mass on the Standard Model's predicted top quark mass, we employed a two-step fitting process.  First, we fitted the Standard Model's predicted t\ \bar{t} cross-section as a function of the top quark mass using precise CDF II measurements.  Subsequently, we incorporated the measured W mass from CDF II along with the fitted top quark mass into a two-dimensional chi-squared fit with experimental data on the t\ \bar{t}$ cross-section and branching fractions.  Our results indicate that the measured W mass from CDF II induces a significant deviation in the predicted top quark mass from its previously estimated value, with the top quark mass now estimated to be approximately 172.94 GeV.  However, it's worth noting that the CDF II Collaboration has since revised the W mass to 173.21$\pm$0.16\,GeV, a value that, when combined with other LHC measurements of the t\ \bar{t}$ mass threshold, suggests a prediction of approximately 173.18 GeV for the top quark mass.

Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
submitted by users, posing a challenge in deciding which ones to prioritize and respond to.
To facilitate maintenance, especially in large-scale systems, researchers proposed
the CQH approach, which allows developers to submit change requests online and
automatically determines relevant quantum queries from user inputs in response to
various maintenance tasks. A recent study examined the CQH approach in the context 
of handling change requests on GitHub. Notably, our analysis revealed that developers
struggle to select suitable search terms from user-submitted change requests, and
existing search term suggestions fail to meet the needed quality. Furthermore, our
analysis showed that CQH's information retrieval component is not heavily utilized,
as only 5% of possible calls were made. Overall, our analysis provides valuable insights
into integrating CQH to ease the process of maintaining software systems.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, researchers analyzed acoustic characteristics like speaking pace and pitch variation. By comparing the degrees to which speakers converged with their counterparts, researchers found that some individuals were more easily synchronized to than others. Furthermore, when studying speaker pairs in natural conversations, it was observed that those more easily synchronized to also tended to mirror each other's vocal traits early on in the interaction. This correspondence between speakers' acoustic characteristics and adaptation patterns offers valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of conversational synchronization.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). This
collection offers customizable visualizations and comprehensive access to our
dataset, consisting of 800,000 galaxy spectra spanning six redshift intervals,
which can be explored by galaxy type or properties. These tools are also
incorporated into our online interface, allowing users to dissect and interact
with the data across various scales. Furthermore, we illustrate their potential
by showcasing a detailed analysis of the distant galaxy S2-1404.

Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. Therefore, we present a novel, unsupervised method, called SSCAP, that identifies likely temporal segments across a variety of videos without the need for explicit annotation. SSCAP utilizes self-supervised learning techniques to derive distinguishing features from videos and a novel action parsing approach that identifies correlations among activity sub-components while accurately determining their sequential progression. The effectiveness of SSCAP is demonstrated through its exceptional performance on classic datasets (Breakfast and 50Salads) as well as a larger-scale dataset (ActivityNet) in the context of action parsing only. Furthermore, SSCAP outperforms existing approaches on weakly-supervised Salads and Breakfast when fine-tuned without additional information. The proposed method is made publicly available to the research community at https://github.com/TCohmb/SSCAP.

We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar{D}^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create associated interpolating currents, and compute their masses, decay constants, and production rates through QCD sum rules. Utilizing current algebra, we then determine their relative production ratios in $\Lambda_b^0$ decays. The study also examines their decay pathways and calculates the branching fractions for these processes. The findings indicate the potential observation in future experiments of $\bar{D} \Sigma_c^{*}$ molecular states with specific quantum numbers.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing techniques. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. To achieve this, we have developed Testing Trainer, an innovative tool leveraging mutation testing and in-class project testing data to facilitate learning. By utilizing Testing Trainer's feedback, which emphasizes sound testing principles, students can refine their test suites, ultimately improving their coding skills and knowledge of testing best practices.

Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to competition or privacy concerns, an alternative approach involves integrating domain adaptation into deep neural network training. Research has shown that demographic bias in training data can be mitigated through a semi-supervised, domain-agnostic learning method that relies solely on target domain examples. Building upon this finding, our innovative demographic bias mitigation technique applies demographic bias removal to an enhanced feature extractor through a mutual enhancement method that utilizes target domain pseudo-labels and demographic attributes. Experimental evaluation on multiple datasets demonstrates that our technique consistently produces consistent performance results, with an average improvement of 7% or more in accuracy compared to other approaches.

A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 MW of electricity within a 200 ton system. This GCR consists of a spherical cavity within a molybdenum-92 enclosure surrounded by a 50 cm thick liquid beryllium reflector, utilizing a fuel mix consisting of 235 UF4, KF, and K. Numerical simulations reveal that the system functions optimally within pressure ranges of 50 to 100 atm. Detailed neutronic assessments were conducted via Monte-Carlo modeling, resulting in crucial insights for determining the required reactor pressure, size, and moderator thickness. Additionally, the study's findings address safety, liquid fuel circulation, heat transfer, and electricity production aspects, thereby rendering additional discussion superfluous. The findings from this research represent a significant step towards establishing a Deep Space operational trajectory for the propulsion nuclear power, paving the way for the development of a self-sustaining space station.

This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localization in time-projection chamber technology for dark matter exploration. Characteristic multivariate observables derived from track projections and coordinates are used to identify spacial clustering among particle interactions. A novel Domain-informed Neural Network architecture, integrating physics-based localization priors into neural networks, is developed and trained for enhanced accuracy and generalization in spacial localization, as well as time-ordering using a range of multivariate observables. Localization results for O(100) kiof events are analyzed, demonstrating a 10-fold improvement in precision for spacial localization and a 5-fold improvement for time-ordering using the Domain-informed Neural Network, with results applicable to a wide range of dark matter research and particle physics applications.

The development of models for stellar, substellar, and planetary atmospheres heavily relies on accurate input data, specifically the detailed molecular absorption data necessary for a consistent understanding of atmospheric spectra. In this context, the MOLSPIT project has concentrated on compiling a comprehensive, consistent, and precise molecular absorption database for a wide range of temperatures (3000-6700 K) using the LT-2.5 database, specifically tailored for the SPIRou spectrograph. By leveraging the AURELIE code for the construction of the database, the MOLSPIT project's findings are significant: (i) discrepancies exist between molecular absorption cross-sections; (ii) the choice of atomic and molecular data influences model results and atmospheric spectrum simulations; (iii) the inclusion of geometric progression in line lists affects the accuracy of model flux and transmission calculations, particularly in the case of SPIRou's operating conditions; (iv) the systematic comparison of model atmospheres developed using the MOLSPIT, SPIRou, and ACCRETESpec databases reveals both similarities and differences in their respective properties and fluxes; (v) the analysis of the most accurate models shows a general agreement regarding the shape of the iron absorption band, but with a generally broader line profile in the case of hotter models compared to those of cooler models.

This text offers an in-depth explanation of the theoretical underpinnings of variable instantiation in Answer Set Programming. We define a specific type of operator, well-founded grounding algorithms rely on, and examine its behavior further. Building on this, we develop a formal framework for modeling language semantics, which we use to investigate the relationship between semantics and model operators. This provides a complete characterization of programs that can be resolved using the ASP resolution rule. Additionally, we establish a connection between the model operators' behavior and Answer Sets, which we leverage to create a universal model operator. This allows us to express any fixed-point definition using this operator, making it possible to determine if a given program has an Answer Set. As a result, we derive decidability results for checking the existence of Answer Sets and satisfiability.

We have extended quantum resource theories to encompass complex scenarios with multiple intertwined resources that dictate the behavior of physical systems. By formulating interconversion conditions for these resources, we have developed a generalisation of the first law of thermodynamics. Our investigation into multi-resource theories led us to discover the crucial role of relative entropy in measuring the transformation of resources. The first law now represents a unifying framework for both individual resources and multi-resource theories, highlighting its fundamental significance. Moreover, we have shown that thermodynamic implementation of resource freebiding is limited by entropy rates of resource trade-offs.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large-scale time series data, even when individual trends are linked. Our approach is based on a method that measures how much each part of a time series is driven by chance. When there are stochastic trends, some of these driving forces have real causes, but others can be attributed to random fluctuations. By examining the distribution of these random factors, we can determine the number of underlying trends. However, in a typical situation, the number of random patterns cannot be precisely known. To address this issue, we propose a more straightforward method that focuses only on the most obvious trends. Specifically, we discard a certain number of the lowest Eigen values, where'm' is the number of underlying trends, and 'k' is a value that represents how well each trend is influenced by chance. By examining the change in patterns in the remaining data, we can identify the number of underlying trends. When applied to economic data, this method shows that a single random pattern cannot be discarded, and that multiple underlying trends are likely to exist. Interestingly, the number of underlying trends cannot be precisely determined. Nevertheless, our results suggest that these trends are likely to be only a few.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, incorporating explicit designs that enable linear time decoding processes. The construction is based on a specific combinatorial structure involving vertices, edges, and faces, defined within a Cayley complex framework. A novel algorithm is described for determining the code parameters, and analysis is provided to assess the potential threshold values for this code design. Notably, dense sublattices are identified in the code's supported space, facilitating direct application of established algorithms from classical coding theory, including those related to random sampling and Fourier sampling. Following an initial purification step, a specific form of quantum error correction, involving a unitary transformation, can be performed on any given noise channel. Critical aspects of this code design, including its ability to operate beneath a specific threshold for the probability of errors, are discussed. Specifically, this code can operate below the Dewey-Nayak threshold despite not being a quantum surface code. Furthermore, a specific form of error correction, involving a unitary transformation, can be performed on any given noise channel, and the code can operate beneath a specific threshold for the probability of errors, making it suitable for practical quantum computing applications.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, alongside its related covering problems, remains relatively unstudied within distributed computation settings despite being well-understood in sequential models. Notably, results on high girth graphs have established the difficulty of distributed domination, leading us to explore the problem within a specific subset of these graphs characterized by high girth and specific diameter restrictions. Our study introduces a new lower bound for distributed domination by showing a Ω(n^2 / (r + 1)) time complexity inequality on bipartite k-girth graphs with a constant diameter of 3, and further narrowing this down to a Ω(n^2 / r) time complexity inequality for the specific case where the graph has a constant girth of 4 and diameter of 4.

This research examines the impact of disorder on the correlation between Green's functions in two-dimensional topological insulators of higher order. We demonstrate that disorder does not disrupt the scaling logodds continuity, which ensures the protection of corner states in scenarios involving disorder. Additionally, we find that disorder does not disrupt the scaling logodds continuity for bulk bound states within these materials. A random Hamiltonian field characterization of correlation's scaling logodds continuity is also developed. Moreover, we establish that bulk bound states scale logodds continuity is equivalent to the localization of the eigenstates of the Green's function around the disorder average Green's function. If necessary, refer to the accompanying notebook for implementation details.

A search for a heavy gluino with a range of masses is being conducted, focusing on scenarios predicted by specific supersymmetry theories, including ones involving high-mass states and scenarios with compressed mass spectra. The study used 139 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at 13 TeV by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. It targets final states featuring multiple jets and one or two poorly identified jets, and examines two signatures: a single massive jet with $b$-quark origins and a pair of massive jets. For three exclusive sets of scenarios, the study observed no excess above standard model predictions, thereby tightening existing limits on gluino masses within these scenarios: it now places a lower mass limit of 2.0 TeV in the high-mass case, 1.23 TeV in the high-mass splittance case, and 937 GeV in the compressed mass case, all under the assumption of medium-to-high degree of jet mass uncertainty. Additionally, the study provides new results from scenarios involving transverse single-top-quark vector boson production for the first time.

Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally achieves accurate reproduction of view-dependent phenomena by densely sampling a scene from multiple viewpoints. However, most light field-based methods struggle to model view-invariant or dynamic information, such as occlusions and 3D textures. In our study, we develop a model that interprets a light field as 5D: 4D for light field rendering and an additional temporal dimension for handling dynamics. Since most real-world light fields are sparse and irregular, we design a neural network that learns to complete the light field from a few examples, leveraging its inherent structure. Our approach, dubbed LAFIS, utilizes a geometric representation, combining both 3D and 2D projections into a 4D light field, making LAFIS efficient with minimal view samples. Our method also incorporates a self-supervised loss, which further enhances performance by leveraging occlusion relationships across views. Evaluation on and off shelf ping-pong pairs as well as semi-synthetic datasets demonstrates significant improvements, with LAFIS delivering state-of-the-art results using a fraction of the resources compared to prior methods, including deepfs-recon and deepview.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

We are investigating chiral celestial algebras found in celestial holography by using self-dual Yang-Mills theory and self-dual gravity formulated under the light-cone gauge, along with exploring an extension of the latter. Furthermore, the previously mentioned w1+∞ algebra derived from the soft expansion of the diffeomorphism algebra that represents the kinematic algebra plays a significant role. Also a related central extension of the k∗ algebra that combines both the Poincaré and Galilean algebras in their respective contexts appears in both gravity and Yang-Mills theory. Additionally, the w1+∞-generated tree-level scattering amplitudes follow the colour-kinematics duality.

A powerful and dynamic solar eruption triggered by shock waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the formation of type II radio bursts. These spectacular events occur when a shock wave probably triggered by a streamer or a loop collapses, causing a rapid increase in density. As the shock wave steams ahead, it may compress both magnetic fields and plasma repeatedly, creating areas of enhanced magnetic field and electron beams that can accelerate electrons in large quantities, as seen in the occurrence of steep radio frequency bursts accompanying type II radio bursts. 

However, the exact mechanism utilized by shocks in compressing magnetic fields despite their substantial relative motions remains unknown, especially in fluids where magnetic fields play a crucial role. Consequently, researchers created a simulation model incorporating magnetic fields to study shock-compression mechanisms. They found that although magnetic fields do not affect shock propagation, they diminish significantly behind the shock wave. As a result, the magnetic energy decreases and transferred to the plasma energy. Consequently, the plasma loses its ability to follow the shock wave, creating a considerable discrepancy between the shock wave's speed and the way ions and electrons move.

This phenomenon explains the observed steep radio frequency bursts in numerous studies. Furthermore, the phenomenon highlights the complexities of interactions between shocks, magnetic fields, and the Sun's plasma. To further clarify the mechanisms, researchers suggested that future type II radio burst simulations be conducted under realistic conditions, including consideration of the Sun's magnetic fields and varying densities.

A detailed likelihood analysis is performed on the general two Higgs doublet model in order to assess its ability to explain observed anomalies in rare decays of $B$ mesons, particularly the anomalies associated with $b\to c l \overline{\nu}$ and $b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ transitions. This analysis finds that the model effectively addresses the anomalies associated with $b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ transitions and is capable of providing a $1\sigma$ fit to the experimental data on the $R(D^{(*)})$ ratios, though it fails to account for specific anomalous signatures in the $B_{q}\to K^{*}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ and $B_{q}\to K\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decay processes. This finding prompts an investigation into potential sources of these discrepancies, revealing a correlation between the $C_{9}(m_{b})$ and $C_{10}(m_{b})$ coefficients that could explain the anomalies, as well as a discrepancy between theoretical predictions and experimental data for the $F_{L}$ fraction in $B\to K^{*}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decays. Furthermore, this analysis highlights additional constraints that can be placed on the model, thereby reducing the allowed parameter space for the $C_{7}/C_{9}$ ratio, even without considering some of the most restrictive data inputs.

This study introduces a unique, self-contained three-dimensional random vortex system that mirrors the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations for non-viscous incompressible fluid flows. The newly developed random vortex system incorporates a stochastic differential equation that interacts with a finite-dimensional functional differential equation, contrasting it with earlier two-dimensional random vortex dynamics equations. The creation of this random vortex system lays the groundwork for developing innovative numerical techniques, known as random vortex methods, for solving three-dimensional incompressible fluid flow equations through Monte Carlo simulations. In order to establish the three-dimensional random vortex dynamics equations, we have formulated two influential methods: first, the duality of the conditional distributions of two interconnected Taylor diffusions, offering an integration by parts technique in the context of path space; second, a forward type Feynman-Kac formula that expresses solutions to nonlinear parabolic equations as a form of functional integration. The random vortex system dynamics equations are an adaptation of earlier two-dimensional research, including a study by Oster, where the vortex system was based on semilinear heat equations, as well as a study by Liu and Xiong, who explored the combination of two-dimensional Taylor diffusions and linear functional differential equations.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be described using complex random variables associated with each input mode. The entropy of this state vector serves as a measure of its uncertainty. Research has shown that the maximum entropy is directly proportional to the number of modes used. Specifically, a study has found a logarithmic relationship between the maximum entropy and the number of modes. This entropy also exhibits a dimensionless constant. To verify these results experimentally, a boson sampling device with a variable number of modes was implemented using single photons and mini-economical spatial modes. The constant's value was found to be close to the theoretically predicted value of $\ln(2.79)$, providing an approximation of $\ln(2.78)\pm\ln(2.80)$. This experiment's findings are in line with theoretical expectations. The development of a boson sampling device with a variable number of modes paves the way for exploring the statistics of complex systems.

Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping that captures temporal variation while prioritizing sample distinctions and learning a grid's predictive structure. By doing so, this novel method integrates a wide range of temporal data types and discovers interactions or pathways between variables that are unique to different stages or states of development/cellular states, and reveals these using just a small number of dimensions. Compared to other temporal sequence analysis approaches, SGTM-TT exhibits superior performance in differentiating between expressions over time, identifying interacting variables, and performing competitive prediction. Additionally, the resulting grid provides unique insights into temporal patterns, and its structure is driven by both variable correlations and differential expression analyses. As a supplementary tool, we developed a web-based interface to provide users with a deeper understanding of the SGTM-TT learning process and its outcomes.

Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a neural network to estimate the value of various states and actions, while some techniques leverage the structure of the target network to improve returns by learning from previous experiences. Although these approaches have significant implications, they were initially designed for markovian settings and are not well-suited for scenarios like online game development, where state transitions are not fully understood. In response to this limitation, this study employs a novel method to interpret the value of state actions in non-markovian contexts by modeling temporal patterns. By analyzing the impact of actions on state transitions and combining these results with the value of current states, this approach aims to improve the efficiency of agents in both markovian and non-markovian environments. Moreover, this method can be integrated with existing algorithms, such as Q-learning, to provide improved performance. The results of both simulation tests and a real-world gaming application show that the proposed network architecture is capable of yielding superior outcomes.

In video action detection, current research often focuses on individual actions within a video, but we're exploring broader possibilities - identifying multiple actions occurring simultaneously in a video. This requires a more comprehensive approach that takes into account not only the individual actions but also their spatial positions and temporal relationships. Based on a theoretical model that views action detection as a process involving object identification and action segmentation, we're working on developing a novel spatiotemporal action detection framework. This framework starts with generating a spatial action map that lists all possible actions in a video and their corresponding spatial coordinates. Then, by leveraging spatial relationships and temporal extrema to represent action context, we employ a novel aggregation method to produce an efficient action template. This can be used to train an end-to-end model that includes both an spatial action localization network and an temporal refinement network, all working together to identify multiple actions occurring simultaneously in a video. Our model has been tested and validated on a range of videos, including actions like "playing guitar" or "frisbee catching," and our experimental results demonstrate significant performance improvements over current state-of-the-art methods.

A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subjected to both qualitative and quantitative analysis in this paper. Key findings indicate that the most challenging transformations for the participating algorithms are extreme cropping, flipping, rotating, and combining images, as well as the use of different color spaces. Notably, the winning approaches employed training with robustly labeled data, state-of-the-art architecture designs, and optimized fusion techniques. The winning strategies were found to perform effectively across a range of difficulty levels, with their top-performing models achieving an average accuracy of 94% across all categories and 96% in the easy transformation group.

Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes' underlying mathematical operators comprise two components: a main, degrading portion that loses its effectiveness at the boundary, specifically in a direction perpendicular to it, along with a smaller, non-degenerate perturbation. Understanding the behavior of such stochastic processes plays a significant role in the stabilization of solutions to associated parabolic equations that incorporate a small parameter. In this context, metastability effects emerge, meaning that as the size of the perturbation approaches zero, the solutions' long-term behavior is dependent on the specific time frame considered. Our study encompasses a range of scenarios, including boundary-value problems under both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. Additionally, we are also investigating periodic homogenization techniques for operators that exhibit degeneracy.

This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) technique, utilizing the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. We discovered that the absence of a magnetic field results in an energy per particle symmetric function in relation to the spin polarization parameter. As a result, our calculations indicate that no spontaneous transition to a ferromagnetic state occurs in nuclear matter under this condition. However, our analysis shows that when magnetic fields of strength $B\gtrsim 10^{18}\ G$ are applied, the symmetry is disrupted and the energy takes on a minimum at a positive spin polarization parameter. Additionally, our calculations indicate that the effect of the magnetic field on the energy value becomes more pronounced at low densities, and the spin polarization parameter exhibits greater sensitivity to magnetic fields under such conditions.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we derived a differential privacy compliant algorithm, which provides quantifiable guarantees. Experimental results show that our approach substantially decreases communication costs while maintaining high data privacy standards.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex was created by combining the observations from GALEX and FIMS, which provided data at nearly identical wavelengths. The UV intensity in the area exhibited significant variation, with diffuse UV radiation largely resulting from dust particles scattering starlight. A UV background intensity of around 1000 CU was measured, with a portion potentially attributed to scattered light in the foreground of dense clouds. Fluorescent hydrogen emissions constituted roughly 10% of total UV intensity across the region, generally corresponding to local continuum levels. A customized radiative transfer model was employed to determine the optical properties of dust particles and cloud geometry in the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex using simulated UV spectra. Model simulations suggested a central brightness of around 5000 CU for the complex's cloud structure, with a dust albedo of around 0.6, corresponding to a single scattering albedo of around 0.75. Additionally, a corresponding optical depth of around 0.1 was predicted, with an estimated amount of dust particles within the complex's cloud structure.

Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research in scientific papers easily accessible to scholars by compiling experimental outcomes and highlighting novel discoveries. Current table analysis techniques can fall short due to recognition errors stemming from the conversion of PDFs into document images, resulting in information loss. This study develops a solution to table extraction by leveraging Graph Neural Networks and incorporates tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document components. An experimental assessment was conducted on a combined dataset from PubLayNet and PubTables-1M to evaluate the proposed approach's efficacy.

This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds. Building on this concept, our study provides a complete characterization of the dynamic CH solution for two-person dirty faces games. Notably, our findings indicate that lower-level players learn and incorporate higher-level opponents' characteristics over time. Furthermore, our results suggest that dynamic CH equates to a form of bayesian learning with limited memory (LLM) and converges to a static CH equilibrium as the game progresses. A mathematical proof was established, and supporting simulation evidence is presented.

Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches incorporating remote sensing data and microcensus statistics. We conducted an experiment in Mozambique, specifically estimating the population count in two districts between censuses. Furthermore, we evaluated the feasibility of leveraging open-access datasets to support population forecasting. Our exploration also involved utilizing existing annotated datasets to improve building footprint prediction, coupled with additional annotation of 'dot' features from targeted areas to enhance accuracy. We found that population estimates improved when utilizing estimated building footprint areas derived from this method over solely using available features.

Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as cuckoo and xor filters. Moreover, adaptive solutions have recently been introduced, enabling the maintenance of a filter's properties even in the presence of deletions. This research further innovates by introducing two innovative techniques called Ari and Ari2. These approaches integrate arithmetic codes with balanced hash tables to reduce false positive rates while maintaining efficient data insertion speeds.ari filters are designed to be compatible with existing systems, including xor and Ari-based filters, allowing them to coexist seamlessly. This flexibility is attributed to the distinct nature of Ari codes in comparison to xor codes. This study also showcases the efficacy of these innovative filters through experiments conducted on real-world data sets, showcasing their superiority in balancing speed and memory utilization.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms. This process draws parallels with renowned dark-state coherent control techniques. In our study, we also explored the impact of several collisional mechanisms on the formation of atom-molecule pairs in a well-defined experimental context. Furthermore, we examined how entanglement between atoms is generated during this conversion via the creation of three-body clusters and associated dark states.

Zhang et al. initially introduced a multi-resolution SPH method to analyze fluid-structure interactions while maintaining efficiency, accuracy, and robustness. 
In the present study, their SPH framework, incorporating diverse spatial-temporal resolutions for individual components, is extended to include multi-phase flows, particularly with significant density discrepancies, interacting with rigid or deformable structures. 
To achieve this, a straightforward multi-phase model was developed, incorporating varying density reinitialization strategies instead of employing separate formulations to enforce mass conservation in the lighter and heavier phases. 
Additionally, a modified transport velocity formulation was proposed to reduce artificial voids and unrealistic phase separation by introducing a local background pressure that depends on the flow state over time.
A Riemann-based boundary condition is utilized to address FSI coupling, particularly in the context of the triple point in single- and multi-resolution frameworks. 
Several numerical simulations, which entail multi-phase flows with substantial density ratios and intricate interfaces, as well as multi-phase FSI scenarios, demonstrate the enhanced efficiency, precision, and robustness of the presented method. 
Comparisons with the results of Zhang et al. in the context of single-phase FSI underscore the benefits of this SPH framework in efficiently handling complex multi-physics problems.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, contributing significantly to advancements in the field. Despite machine learning's impressive capabilities, its processing efficiency can be improved upon by leveraging quantum computing's advantages. This paper explores the application of quantum machine learning, focusing on the intersection of quantum sensing and simulation. Within quantum sensing, we delve into the use of machine learning for simulating spin dynamics and modeling noise in quantum systems, while in quantum simulation, we examine how machine learning can determine the parameters of quantum systems from simulated or experimental data. Additionally, we highlight the potential benefits of this hybrid approach in preparing quantum processors for practical applications and potentially achieving supremacy in certain tasks.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it isn't perfect because it can't guarantee that the synthesized speech sounds natural when it's used. In order to enhance FastPitch's capabilities, an easy method to change pitch without affecting the voice's unique tone while training FastPitch was developed. This method employs two algorithms: a simple pitch-shifting technique and a voice modification technique. By combining these methods, a new version of FastPitch was created that can easily and effectively change pitch without affecting the voice's tone. Listen-only tests have shown significant improvements in speech quality and recognition rates, exceeding those of the original FastPitch. Furthermore, tests that included visual cues led to better results. This new version's quality and recognition rates surpass those of the original FastPitch and other similar models in all tests conducted.

This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object reasoning problems through
video comprehension, identified as a underdeveloped task in current computer vision.
A key challenge of this task lies in understanding object permanence, namely that objects
continue to exist behind obstacles. To address this challenge, we present the Perm+
dataset, comprising 5,371 videos of animal species, accompanied by annotations detailing
object locations, intersections, and transformations across time. A proposed model,
PRAVI, leverages a novel Attention via Transformation network, which uses transformation
predictions to manipulate attention masks and sample relevant frames for reasoning.
Experimental evaluations and analysis indicate that PRAVI effectively implements
object permanence reasoning in video comprehension tasks.

We have conducted a precise calculation of neutral-current Drell-Yan production, considering the full complexity of QCD and the presence of bottom quarks. Our study serves as a reference for the 2015 update of the PDFs by the NNPDF collaboration and includes detailed predictions for the Z boson and W boson across a broad range of energy levels. To facilitate accurate comparisons with experimental results, our computation is presented in a format that matches the structure of published data from the LHC. A notable aspect of our findings is the significant impact of bottom quarks on the scale dependence of the predicted rates, particularly for the Z boson, as well as the corresponding effects on parton distribution functions and their uncertainty estimates.

Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields like healthcare and education. This research develops a realistic QoE metric to evaluate the quality of the remote navigation experience. By considering the remote operator's navigation skills, visual communication quality, and physical interaction, the proposed metric provides an comprehensive quality of experience score. Based on existing quality of experience models, a new synthesis formula is created to predict the QoE score in different scenarios. Additionally, a study involving 30 participants was conducted to validate the formula and assess various factors influencing the QoE score, such as visual delay, physical interaction accuracy, and remote operator skill level.

In this study, we revisit the core features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, thoroughly analyzing their full probabilistic frameworks, including the conditional distributions for each parameter. We extend these models to incorporate a linear relationship between the second-stage mean and a set of relevant predictor variables. The implementation details of the employed Gibbs sampling algorithms are thoroughly described, which are essential for generating samples when estimating model parameters. Furthermore, a real-world example examines the effect of nitrogen soil concentration and a categorical variable (farm) on plant size.

The game "Mafia," also known as "Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the main groups. Each phase in the game, consisting of day and night segments, allows for various actions to take place, with a specific sequence. Mafia members have special abilities, while citizens have none. Researchers investigated the chances of the mafia's victory and the citizens' victory under specific terms and conditions. Initially, they found that under a particular set of terms and conditions with varying participant numbers, the chances of the mafia's victory and the citizens' victory both increase as the number of mafia members increases. This led them to explore under what conditions the game's outcome would be equal for both groups. This new investigation revealed two important findings - first, the chances of the mafia's victory and the citizens' victory are both equal when half of the mafia members have a specific ability to a certain number of citizens, and second, the chances of the mafia's victory and the citizens' victory are both equal when the number of mafia members is the square root of the total number of participants.

Several planetary systems have multiple giant planets, and research aims to
understand how their formation is affected when planets develop in tandem. Our
study uses long-term computer simulations of planetary growth from a shared gas
disk, and the results reveal a link between planet mass ratios and the onset of
gas accreting. If the inner planet begins gas accreting sooner, it tends to grow
faster and heavier than the outer planet. However, if the outer planet starts
accriving gas first, it often outmasses the inner planet. To replicate the
planetary configurations observed in real systems, our study shows how the mass
ratios can be influenced by slight discrepancies in the timing of gas
accrivation, on the order of 0.1 million years. Additionally, our study
indicates that planets may start gas accreting while still wrapped in protoplanetary
disks, and that this process can continue even after the disk has disappeared.

The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials on a macroscopic scale
depends on intricate electronic transport mechanisms involving the constituent
nanoscale objects. Heat units known as phonons exhibit a dual influence on
conductivity: by scattering electrons, they can hinder it but can also enhance it
by facilitating electron propagation through a complex energy terrain. 
In our investigation, we have observed a temperature-dependent, coherent electron
transfer between neighboring nanotubes through measurements of local electrical
resistance under controlled heat application. Our analysis reveals the presence
of two temperature ranges: one characterized by resistance increase due to elevated
electron scattering by phonons that maintain electron localization at tube walls,
and another where these phonons facilitate coherent electron sharing between tubes.
As temperature approaches 100 K, the intertube coherence emerges as a transferring
current across the system.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple datasets. The algorithm is specifically designed for datasets consisting of samples from different groups, known as 'heterogeneous datasets'. FkMHS aims to overcome several limitations of current clustering methods that fail to accommodate multi-sample data and inconsistent dataset sizes. Firstly, it weights the influence of individual datasets based on their size, ensuring equal cluster assignments for each. Secondly, it assigns distinct weights to various features, selecting important ones for clustering. Finally, it uses a logarithmic weighting coefficient for partitioning each sample across datasets, thus adapting to varying dataset sizes. The effectiveness of FkMHS is evaluated using six data sets from the UCI machine learning repository, with compared analyses of eight competing methods demonstrating its superior performance. Additionally, the reliability and generalizability of the model are assessed using five validation indices and a battery of testing methods.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of non-linear functions. This new algorithm uniquely estimates expert parameters through an analysis of the cross-moment tensor between inputs and outputs. While it still necessitates an EM algorithm to recover gating parameters, the proposed approach simplifies this process and significantly improves convergence compared to existing methods, leading to enhanced performance on both simulated and real-world data sets when compared to standard baselines.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry.

While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the Cosmic Microwave Background may signify a previously undiscovered, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in nature. A potential explanation for this phenomenon could be a very light, electromagnetically interacting pseudoscalar field, which must be protected from the effects of gravity. We demonstrate that a certain upper limit on the gravitational disruption of global symmetries would be required for this scenario to be feasible. Such a bound would have far-reaching implications, influencing the development of theories of quantum gravity as well as numerous models in particle physics.

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. These findings were further confirmed by cross-checking the source's cluster membership using Gaia data and proper motions. Our FUV-optical diagrams indicate that NGC 4147 contains 1,431 members, including 1,030 sources from the FUV band and 701 sources from the Gaia dataset. Our investigations reveal a prominent FUV-excess region in the cluster's center, comprising both blue horizontal branch stars and blue straggler stars. After eliminating Galactic blue horizontal branch imitation sources, we analyzed the FUV-to-ultraviolet color-magnitude diagrams to identify the location of BHS. Conversely, BNS were identified in the Gaia colour-magnitude diagrams. Our calculations also analyze the structural parameters of NGC 4147, revealing a slight difference in the radii obtained from the FUV and Gaia datasets. Furthermore, we discovered 134 new proposed variable sources, including 76 shrouded sources, using Fourier sine terms. Our findings indicate that NGC 4147 contains a total of 8.53 x 10^4 stars, along with a determined radial density profile that indicates a population gradient in the cluster.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) to draw from the expertise developed in source domains and apply it effectively to new target domains, even if they have different distributions. By pre-training the DNNs on source domains and then fine-tuning them on target domains, DTL makes it possible to leverage trained models without sacrificing performance. Despite these benefits, there are significant challenges associated with adapting the pre-trained models to new applications. This challenge is characterized by a tradeoff between model performance and interpretability. This study will review recent advancements in DTL, along with the associated computational and theoretical intricacies. The key techniques will be classified into three main categories: data normalization, network flexibility, and statistical similarity assessment. The paper will also investigate potential methods to enhance the transferability of the pre-trained DNNs. These methods include utilizing common training objectives, applying data enhancement techniques widely used in the industry, and developing new theories based on the principle of minimum statistical complexity. Moreover, we will discuss how the complexity of the models can be estimated quantitatively. Some critical issues will also be addressed, such as the potential theory-related flaws in the current DTL framework. This study will also demonstrate the progress made in using DTL for a specific application: the analysis of physiological signals using the DTL-based hyperparameter optimization technique. Finally, we will reflect on the most significant challenges still facing the DTL framework and the opportunities it presents for

In various scenarios, such as mobilization, pandemic mitigation, and advertising, the swift dissemination of information and social behaviors are paramount. Despite thorough examinations of massive cascade dynamics across multiple contexts, few have scrutinized the impact of network structure on information propagation efficiency. Our research applies a theoretical framework to both artificial and real-world networks, investigating the effect of network modularity on information diffusion rate in massive cascade models. Additionally, we delve into the influence of clustering coefficient, which is particularly relevant in network evolution studies. Our findings indicate that network modularity significantly influences information propagation efficiency and that focusing on local information in diffusion strategies is often counterproductive. Contrary to expectations, real-world networks exhibit a complex relationship between clustering coefficient, volatility, and information quality. Specifically, for clusters smaller than a certain threshold, increasing clustering coefficient detrimentalizes information propagation, whereas clustering coefficients exceeding that threshold facilitate efficient information propagation.

Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we derive numerical measures indicating the proximity of two Lagrangians based on their angular separation, and this is applied specifically to unit Lagrangians that resemble circles. These measures depend on angles and angles derived from angles, and it is proven that they can be related to measures comparing surfaces called cylinders. Furthermore, it is proven that under certain conditions, these measures are equivalent, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Consequently, this result enables the reevaluation of certain principles in Hamiltonian Floer theory.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard method of perturbation
is numerically investigated through a systematic approach using random variable phasing, alongside
empirical evidence. The distance between distinct nonlinear interference points is found to effectively
estimate the channel's memory order when the memory rank is less than half the channel's length.
Conversely, when the memory order exceeds this threshold, relying solely on the distance between distinct
interference points is deemed insufficient for accurate estimation. An alternative approach is therefore
proposed, where a generalized version of the Levenshtein distance is applied to a subset of the channel's output
sequences, followed by investigation into its performance when noise is introduced to finite-length inputs of
communication channels for various memory configurations.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. Unfortunately, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on the Android platform, where hackers modify the entire malicious application or create a new one from scratch to evade detection. The study begins with an overview of Android malware detection and various evasion attacks, followed by a detailed analysis of problem-space attacks. It then discusses the challenges in implementing these attacks without compromising their effectiveness. The paper also introduces an integrated approach that utilizes a multi-objective optimization algorithm to guide the evolution of mutated malware samples in a problem-space context. This approach optimizes both the quality of modified code and the difficulty in reversing engineered the malware's functionality. The experiment results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in crafting sophisticated malware that evades detection successfully.

Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as processes. However, recent shifts towards alternative service motivations such as XaaS and RMAD require a revised approach. Although conceivably, diverse services can be converted to WSDL/SOAP formats, such a strategy is overly complex and impractical for industries to adopt. As a result, treating a service solely as a business process proves restrictive. Conversely, we view a service as a procedure that is agnostic to specific technologies, decoupled, and transparent to locations. Underpinned by these ideas, we introduce Ozy, a generalized orchestration framework, enabling us to redefine the orchestration architecture using established technologies. Our definition allows the creation of flexible, modular, and adjustable structures within Ozy. Moreover, we introduce the concept of procedure independence, enabling the use of multiple processes within the same instance, thus providing greater adaptability for the integration of diverse services. Our framework has been applied in the development of several applications.

Recent experimental verification of the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian topological order, despite theoretical predictions of its thermal Hall conductivity being even, suggests an odd thermal Hall conductivity. We propose that an internal degree of freedom within the Pfaffian wave function causes the time reversal symmetry to become effective only at this internal degree of freedom level, thereby accounting for the observed odd thermal Hall conductivity. As evidence for this assertion, an experimental investigation of the thermal Hall effect in the same sample that exhibits the Pfaffian topological order, but at a temperature that is lower than the gap temperature, is recommended. If the observed thermal Hall conductivity transitions from even to odd as the temperature decreases, it could serve as additional proof for the Pfaffian's internal symmetry structure.

We develop a comprehensive model for the formation of Thakurta black holes, which originate from the direct collapse of gas in isolated regions. By simulating the formation process, we find that it occurs when the kinetic energy density exceeds the magnetic energy density, and the gas density exceeds the threshold for star formation. This novel black hole formation mechanism is unique in that it doesn't involve the conventional collapse of a massive star formed from gas. Our analysis indicates that such Thakurta black holes have masses between $10^{5}$ and $10^{10} M_{\odot}$, and can accumulate at the center of galaxies along with supermassive black holes, eventually merging with them. The Thakurta black holes can also be ejected into satellite galaxies as a consequence of galaxy mergers, where they can persist for billions of years. The possibility of detecting these Thakurita black holes in near future is also explored.

The complexity of gaps and ring formations in protoplanetary discs indicates pressure hotspots connected to ongoing planet formation and other factors, with hydrodynamic models predicting widespread presence of ring-like dust structures in these systems. Recent studies of such dust structures in TW Hya and other systems suggest they may be caused by disc hacking due to planet formation. However, mathematical models of disc evolution show that disc hacking can only occur when a system has sufficiently massive dust particles, with a minimum mass of about 0.3 milligrams, to prevent the pressure pressure hotspots from being erased by kinetic disc hacking. These models also show that planet formation is likely to occur at pressure pressure hotspots. For systems like TW Hya, with disc hacking due to planet formation, dust ring formations may be caused by disc hacking by multiple growing protoplanets, with potential implications for planetary formation and mass distribution.

Extremely large, overparameterized models have achieved impressive success. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations inherent to the learner itself. We also examine whether these constraints are exacerbated under robust learning conditions. Our study indicates that this is indeed the case. We demonstrate specific learning tasks for which learners with computational limitations need significantly more parameters than those with theoretical information bounds. Moreover, our results suggest that robust learning could necessitate even more parameters. Building upon a recent discovery, we utilized Kolmogorov complexity to simulate these constraints, and then proved that under certain conditions, the necessary number of parameters is directly proportional to the computational complexity involved. To validate our theoretical findings, we successfully applied Kolmogorov complexity to predict the optimal number of parameters for real-world tasks. Our empirical experiments, involving artificial and natural language tasks, show that learners needing to simulate computational complexity require substantially more parameters than those not required to, essentially, compute their training data.

Three results concerning the presence of Bohr sets in threefold sumsets have been proven. More specifically, considering a countable discrete abelian group $G$ and commuting endomorphisms $\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3$ whose images have finite indices, we demonstrate that 
  (1) For a set $A \subset G$ with positive upper Banach density and satisfying the condition that the sum of its images under the given endomorphisms is zero, there exists a Bohr set within the sum of its images under the individual endomorphisms. This generalizes theorems previously established for $\mathbb{Z}$ by Bergelson and Ruzsa as well as the results obtained by the primary author for pairs of endomorphims. 
  (2) The same conclusion as in (1) applies when $A$ has Banach density one and for which there is no element $g \in G$ such that the sum of its images under the given endomorphisms equals $g$. 
  (3) For a set $A \subset G$ of Banach density one and for all $g \in G$, there is either found a Bohr set within the sum of its images under the given endomorphisms or a set $B \subset A$ with Banach density one such that the sum of the images of $B$ under the given endomorphisms is not a

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify potential improvements, ultimately yielding substantial computational savings up to 87.5%. Furthermore, our approach enables the detection of tight lower bounds in a considerable proportion of instances, revealing that default heuristic methods can produce near-optimal results in a wide range of scenarios.

This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing limitations in current methods which struggle with modality-noise and modality-missing. We introduce K3M, a novel method incorporating knowledge modality to mitigate noise and supplement missing modalities in image and text data. K3M utilizes a modal-encoding layer and a modal-interaction layer that combines features of individual modalities with a structured aggregation module fusing knowledge, image, and text modalities. Through pretraining with MOM, MLM, and LPM tasks, we demonstrate K3M outperforms existing methods in handling modality-noise or modality-missing scenarios in E-commerce product datasets and related downstream tasks.

A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, particularly in non-linear exploration. A novel exploration approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), offers superior results, but its variations struggle to maintain dimensional stability. We present a novel form of DIM that consistently extracts dimension-specific information without undergoing internal transformations, thereby making it highly suitable for neuroimaging analysis. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in three applications, namely, brain segmentation, tumor classification, and adaptive dimension reduction, where it consistently outperforms traditional DIM. Our findings show that the stability of unsupervised learning, particularly in dimension exploration, can significantly impact its overall performance.

Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, which sequential models efficiently handle, though their connection to linguistic semantics in output predictions often falls short. This study presents an innovative score called I-score, an efficient search algorithm termed Backward Dropping Algorithm, and an innovative feature engineering technique known as the "dagger technique". Firstly, the paper introduces I-score, an innovative score that identifies and prioritizes crucial linguistic semantics for accurate text classification predictions. Subsequently, the paper suggests using Backward Dropping Algorithm to manage dependencies within large datasets. Additionally, the paper proposes "dagger technique" which ensures an optimal association between the input variables and target variable. These methods can be applied universally across feed-forward ANNs, CNNs, and other neural networks, as demonstrated through an experiment using real data from the IMDB where results show significant improvements in accuracy when employing the proposed methods. The experimental findings indicate an notable enhancement in model performance and validation that the proposed methods outperform existing techniques such as Principal Component Analysis and Correlation Coefficient. Furthermore, the paper introduces a new an efficient benchmark for evaluating performance of all kinds of neural networks on text classification task.

We examine the interplay of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model, incorporating both crystal and Coriolis field components. In systems with low dimension, such as a one-dimensional Hubbard model, the interplay leads to a scenario in which the binding of a hole to a doubly occupied site is favored over the inverse process. In a specific context, such as PuTe, this binding becomes more pronounced than the inverse process due to spin-orbit coupling effects. Within a two-dimensional Hubbard model, such as a doped two-dimensional spin-orbit coupled Hubbard model, applicable to systems likeurmoseleiourbide, the effective spin-orbit coupling constant exhibits a significant increase in between quasiparticle peaks. In a paramagnetic state, the spin-orbit coupling constant reaches a maximum at an interaction strength (Utta) that increases with the crystal field, while in an antiferromagnetic state, the (Utta) value is significantly reduced. In a superconducting state, the spin-orbit coupling constant exhibits a reversal, becoming negative below a dimensionality-dependent threshold interaction strength (Uttb) and increasing towards this threshold from below.

A metastable dark matter candidate emerges as a natural consequence of a
confining dynamic, characterized by a mass that exceeds the Universe's age.
This phenomenon is illustrated by the baryon-dark matter interaction through a
derivative coupling. An energy scale, responsible for the interaction strength,
results in dark matter with a variety of long lifetimes across a wide range of
masses. Furthermore, the metastable dark matter candidate shares analogous
features with the "super-dark" candidate proposed in another context.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and efficiently in diverse environments before being released to the public, accurately assessing their performance in varying scenarios is crucial. Given the regulatory restrictions on medical software and the scarcity of comprehensive labeled medical datasets, our approach revolves around predicting a model's performance in an unfamiliar setting using its predicted responses alone, without requiring any modifications to its training process or assumptions about its original data source. This "black-box" model assessment technique is based on conformal prediction and is being evaluated across various medical image datasets and distribution shift scenarios, such as changes in medical institution, imaging technology, or clinical settings. By promoting more effective evaluation methods for AI models, we hope to standardize clinical assessments, enhance AI system robustness and credibility under real-world conditions, and facilitate the development of widely applicable medical AI systems.

High-fidelity simulations involving atomic-level details are now being extensively employed to study nucleic acid structures due to their high precision and resolution in space and time. While this high precision is advantageous, it often results in a computationally demanding process. In simulations conducted over specific timeframes, nucleic acids demonstrate minor changes while generally adhering to their expected behavioral patterns. The present study focuses on nucleic acid simulations employing the CHARMM and AMBER models, with an emphasis on their rotational dynamics. Six rotational parameters, namely, rotation around phosphate group bonds, base pairing, backbone orientation, twist, buckle, and base tilt, are key components that govern nucleic acid structures and are capable of being directly influenced by simulations at the atomic level. Although nucleic acid nucleotides display slight deviations from their expected behavioral patterns, these deviations are well within the bounds of their accepted structural variations. As a result, it has been observed that simulations can be conducted with higher accuracy by reducing the frequency of base pairing updates and allowing more freedom in nucleotide rotations. In fact, the standard sampling of nucleic acid structures, with updates occurring every 10 femtoseconds for phosphate group rotations and base pairing parameters, can result in nucleic acid structures that accurately reflect their expected behavioral patterns. This finding holds true for both DNA and RNA sequences. The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was a significant innovation in entropy encoding developed by Duda, revolutionizing data compression by surpassing the capabilities of arithmetic and Huffman coding. Despite its optimality being studied by Duda et al., the asymptotic redundancy of ANS, relative to the source entropy, remained unclear. In 2022, we introduced the table-based ANS (tANS) variant, which offers a significant advantage in terms of computational efficiency. However, the current tANS encoder is suboptimal due to the additional redundancy it incurs. Our comprehensive analysis focuses on the asymptotic redundancy of the tANS (precise initialization) compared to the source entropy. Our extensive numerical calculations suggest that the tANS redundancy is polynomial in the size of the alphabet $\sigma$, given the constraint that the precision $p$ grows at least as fast as $\sqrt{\sigma}$. Our findings are substantiated by a lower bound on the redundancy proven in this study. These results imply that tANS (imprecise initialization) would incur superlinear redundancy when the alphabet size grows, given the constraint that the precision $p$ grows at most as fast as $\sqrt{\sigma}$.

The dielectric characteristics of micro- and mesoporous materials are heavily influenced by the composition and presence of liquid phases. Electrolyte dielectric behavior is influenced in a complex manner by ion-water and ion-ion interactions, and this phenomenon's intricacies can be better understood with knowledge of respective concentrations. Pore solutions found in cement-based materials are comprised of a complex mixture containing ions from hydration products, chains of polymers within the paste, and a vast array of organic and inorganic substances that may be present. Although the hydrophilic surfaces of pores typically exhibit minimal impact on dielectric behavior at lower concentrations, a contrasting picture emerges at higher ion contents where discrete ion clusters are formed due to electrostatic attractions. In order to investigate and better understand the dielectric characteristics and structural organization within concentrated solutions, we employ advanced theoretical and simulation methods to investigate how ions and molecular-scaled entities are arranged within a confined, complex chemical system such as cement-based cementite. This study leverages molecular dynamics simulations to develop a comprehensive understanding of ion clustering and its connection to dielectric behavior in concentrated solutions. Our analysis of these simulations reveals not only short-range ordering but also longer-range electrostatic attractions that influence the arrangement of these molecules. Furthermore, our examination of the percolation theory applied to these concentrated solutions allows us to track the emergence of longer-range arrangements and the movement of the system from order to a more disordered state on these molecular-scale chemical systems. In our earlier work, the range of heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules was determined, and a predictive model based on resonance saturation was established. This model has been successful in explaining several observed hadronic molecules such as $X(3872)$, $Y(4260)$, and the $P_c$ states, and its predictions for heavy-heavy hadronic molecules seem even more likely. The fact that heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules with the same quantum numbers as the $X(3872)$ can be described by different interactions suggests that those with distinct quantum numbers may consist of diverse components. The predicted masses of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules with the same quantum numbers as the $Y(4260)$ and the $P_c$ states could be around 4400 MeV and 4250 MeV respectively. The discovery of the $Z_b(10610)$ and the $Z_c$ states may imply that the widths of the heavy-heavy hadronic molecules could be larger than those of the heavy-antiheavy ones. The predicted model is consistent with the observed hadronic data. The fact that heavy-antiheavy but not heavy-heavy hadonic molecules are influenced by the tensor couplings of charmed mesons and charmed baryons may imply that the former could decay into the latter. Research on military drones is growing in importance as a swarm can be a
useful asset in warfare, and recent analysis based on 946 studies reveals
who's leading the way and what specific subfields they're focusing on,
